[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering Kubernetes Security: Authentication, RBAC, and Admission Control"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Securing a Kubernetes cluster requires a multi-layered approach. Every request that enters the API server must pass through three distinct phases: Authentication, Authorization, and Admission Control. This tutorial explores how these components work together to protect your cluster."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"Phase 1: Authentication"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Authentication answers the question "Who are you?" The Kubernetes API server relies on client certificates, bearer tokens (such as ServiceAccount tokens), or an external OIDC provider to verify the identity of the user or service account making the request."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Creating a Service Account and Token"},{"order":6,"type":"code","text":"apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: app-deployer
  namespace: production"},{"order":7,"type":"heading","text":"Phase 2: Authorization (RBAC)"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once a request is authenticated, Authorization answers the question "What are you allowed to do?" Kubernetes uses Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) by default. RBAC uses Roles and ClusterRoles to define permissions, and RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings to assign those permissions to users or service accounts."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Defining a Role and RoleBinding"},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  namespace: production
  name: pod-reader
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "watch", "list"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: read-pods
  namespace: production
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: app-deployer
  namespace: production
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io"},{"order":11,"type":"heading","text":"Phase 3: Admission Control"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Admission controllers are pieces of code that intercept requests to the Kubernetes API server prior to persistence of the object, after the request is authenticated and authorized. They can be validating, mutating, or both."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Validating Admission Webhook Example"},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: "image-policy-validator"
webhooks:
- name: "images.example.com"
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    apiVersions: ["v1"]
    operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
    resources: ["pods"]
    scope: "Namespaced"
  clientConfig:
    service:
      namespace: "security-system"
      name: "webhook-service"
      path: "/validate"
  admissionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
  sideEffects: "None"
  timeoutSeconds: 3"},{"order":15,"type":"heading","text":"Summary of Request Flow"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"1. Authentication: Verifies the client credentials and extracts the username and groups."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"2. Authorization: Checks if the user has the required RBAC verbs and resources to execute the action."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"3. Mutating Admission Control: Modifies the incoming request object if necessary (e.g., injecting sidecars)."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"4. Validating Admission Control: Ensures the final state of the object complies with organizational policies before saving to etcd."}]
